title: Symbolic-regression turbulence analysis separates transferable flow physics from dataset-specific closure terms
summary: Using high-fidelity data for plane channels, zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers and adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layers, the authors used symbolic regression to decompose learned turbulence-closure corrections into inner-layer, outer-layer and pressure-gradient components. They report that retaining the generalisable inner-layer term and adding flow-specific corrections improved predictions on held-out boundary-layer and aerofoil configurations, including unseen geometries and Reynolds numbers, outperforming baseline RANS closures in a priori and a posteriori tests. The authors identify conflation of transferable and training-specific flow behavior as a source of poor model generalization in the tested setting.
ai_technology: Symbolic regression applied to high-fidelity turbulence simulation data
organization: Northwestern Polytechnical University; Pennsylvania State University

evidence.tested: Using high-fidelity data for plane channels, zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers and adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layers, the authors used symbolic regression to decompose learned turbulence-closure corrections into inner-layer, outer-layer and pressure-gradient components.
evidence.unknown: The finding concerns model-derived closure components and validation on selected numerical flow configurations, not a new direct physical measurement. The claimed root cause of poor generalization is the authors' conclusion about data-driven turbulence closures in the studied context, not a universal causal theorem about all turbulence models. Out-of-sample tests and comparative RANS simulations support the stated transfer result.
evidence.ai_role: Symbolic regression generated interpretable closure expressions from progressively expanded flow datasets. Decomposition of the learned terms let the researchers distinguish inner-layer components that transferred across flow configurations from outer-layer and pressure-gradient corrections that were specific to flow classes, enabling improved out-of-training-flow predictions.
